title: Glaucoma: protecting remaining vision
intro: Glaucoma damages the optic nerve and can reduce the visual field. The common open-angle form often develops silently. Treatment aims to preserve remaining sight; existing nerve damage usually cannot be reversed.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem
paragraphs: Eye pressure is an important risk factor, but glaucoma can occur with pressure in the usual range. High pressure alone is not the same as established optic-nerve damage.

sections.heading: Assessment and tests
paragraphs: Assessment combines pressure measurement, optic-nerve examination or imaging and visual-field tests. A single normal pressure reading cannot exclude glaucoma; repeat testing may be necessary to establish progression. Bring your medicine list and previous results; ask which findings would change the plan.

sections.heading: Treatment choices
paragraphs: Pressure-lowering drops, laser or surgery are chosen according to type, damage and response. Explain asthma, heart conditions and other medicines because even eye drops can have systemic effects. Agree how benefit and adverse effects will be checked before changing treatment.

sections.heading: Everyday care
paragraphs: Use drops as instructed, avoid touching the bottle tip and ask for a technique demonstration. Tell the team about cost, irritation or missed doses rather than silently stopping treatment. Choose a routine you can maintain, and discuss barriers such as cost, work or language.

sections.heading: Follow-up and warning signs
paragraphs: Attend monitoring even when vision seems unchanged. Sudden painful red eye with blurred vision, halos, headache or nausea needs immediate emergency eye assessment, not a routine appointment.

examples.title: A practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Mira sees clearly but has early field loss on testing. She understands why treatment continues despite having no noticeable symptoms.

examples.title: Another practical example
